'''blunging''' (blun′jing), ''n.''   [Verbal n. of ''blunge'', ''v.'']   The process of mixing clay in potteries.
{{smaller block|The proper amount of the clay and the necessary quantity of water are placed in a trough, and mixed with a blunger, until reduced to a homogeneous mass. In large potteries this work is sometimes done by the machine called a pug-mill.}}

'''blunk'''<sup>1</sup>†, ''v.''   [Origin uncertain; appar. a corruption of ''blenk'' or ''blink''.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To blench; blink; turn aside.

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To spoil; mismanage.   ''Jamieson.'' [Scotch.]

'''blunk'''<sup>2</sup> (blungk), ''n.''   [Cf. ''blunket''.]   In plural, linen or cotton cloths for printing; calicos. [Scotch.]

'''blunker'''<sup>1</sup> (blung′kėr), ''n.''   [< ''blunk''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'', II., + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   A bungler; one who spoils everything he meddles with. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|Dunbog is nae mair a gentleman than the ''blunker'' that’s biggit the bonnie house doun in the howm.
{{right|''Scott'', Guy Mannering, iii.}}}}

'''blunker'''<sup>2</sup> (blung′kėr), ''n.''   [< ''blunk''<sup>2</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   A calico-printer. [Scotch.]

'''blunket†''', ''a.'' and ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''blonket'', ''bloncket'', ''blancket'', < ME. ''blanket'' (a.), ''blunket'', also ''plunket'', ''plonkete'' (n.), appar. < OF. ''blanquet'', var. of ''blanchet'', dim. of ''blanc'', white: see ''blanket'', which is thus a doublet of ''blunket''.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' Gray; grayish or light-blue.
{{smaller block|Our ''bloncket'' liveryes bene all to sadde.
{{right|''Spenser'', Shep. Cal., May.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' A kind of cloth; apparently the same as ''blanket'', 1.

'''blunt''' (blunt), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< ME. ''blunt'', ''blont'', of an edge or point, dull, not sharp; of manner, rude; of mind, dull, stupid, blind; prob. < AS. *''blunt'', found in the deriv. ''Blunta'', a man’s name (cf. the mod. E. surnames ''Blunt'', ''Blount''). The sense of ‘dull, stupid,’ appears to be the orig. one (see the quotation from the Ormulum), pointing to a connection with Icel. ''blunda'' = Sw. ''blunda'' = Dan. ''blunde'', doze, slumber. Cf. ''blunder'', and the sense of ''blunt'' in the quotation from the Prompt. Parv. under ''blunderer''.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Obtuse, thick, or dull, as an angle, edge, or point; having an obtuse, thick, or dull edge or point, as a foil, sword, pencil, etc.; not sharp or acute.
{{smaller block|<poem>No doubt the murtherous knife was dull and ''blunt'',
Till it was whetted on thy stone-hard heart.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Richard III., iv. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|An individual act of wrong sometimes gives a sharp point to a ''blunt'' dagger. {{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Emerson, xiii.}}}}
'''2.''' Dull in understanding; slow of discernment.
{{smaller block|<poem>Unnwis mann iss ''blunnt'' and blind
Off herrtess eghe sihhthe [of heart’s eyesight.]</poem>
{{right|''Ormulum'', l. 16954.}}}}
{{smaller block|His wits are not so ''blunt''. {{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, iii. 5.}}}}
'''3.''' Obtuse; free from sharp angularities, projections, or corners. '''4.''' Rough in manner or speech; rude; unpolished; hence, abrupt in address or manner; plain-spoken; unceremonious: applied to persons.
{{smaller block|<poem>I am no orator, as Brutus is;
But, as you know me all, a plain ''blunt'' man.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', J. C., iii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thou’rt honest, ''blunt'', and rude enough, o’ conscience.
{{right|''Ford'', Lover’s Melancholy, iv. 2.}}}}
'''5.''' Plain; plain-spoken; unceremonious or unconventional; direct; free from circumlocution: as, ''blunt'' truths; a ''blunt'' bearing.
{{smaller block|In ''blunt'' terms, can you play the sorcerer? ''Coleridge.''
To his ''blunt'' manner and to his want of consideration for the feelings of others he owed a much higher reputation for sincerity than he at all deserved.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., vi.}}}}
'''6.''' Hard to penetrate. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|I find my heart hardened and ''blunt'' to new impressions.
{{right|''Pope.''}}}}
'''7†.''' Faint.
{{smaller block|Such a burre myȝt make myn herte ''blunt.''
{{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), i. 176.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn. 4.''' Brusk, bluff, uncivil, rude, uncourteous.}}
'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1†.''' A blunt sword for fencing; a foil.—'''2.''' A needle of a grade shorter and less sharply pointed than a sharp. See ''needle.''—'''3.''' [Slang, and perhaps of different origin.] Money; ready money.
{{smaller block|“Well, how goes it?” said one. “I have been the rounds. The ''blunt’s'' going like the ward-pump.”
{{right|''Disraeli'', Coningsby, ix.}}}}

'''blunt''' (blunt), ''v.''   [< ''blunt, a.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To make blunt, as an edge or point; dull the edge or point of, as a knife or bodkin, by making it thicker.

{{smaller block|A less deadly sword, of which he carefully ''blunted'' the point and edge.{{right|''Macaulay'', Addison.}}}}
{{smaller block|Knowledge neither ''blunts'' the point of the lance, nor weakens the arm that wields a knightly sword.{{right|''Ticknor'', Span. Lit., I. 334.}}}}
'''2.''' To weaken or deaden, as appetite, desire, or power of the mind; impair the force, keenness, or susceptibility of.
{{smaller block|''Blunt'' not his love.{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., iv. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|To ''blunt'' or break her passion.{{right|''Tennyson'', Lancelot and Elaine.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To become blunt: as, the blade ''blunts'' easily.

'''blunthead''' (blunt′hed), ''n.'' An East Indian serpent, ''Amblycephalus boa'', of the family ''Colubridæ'' and subfamily ''Leptognathinæ'', of Java, Borneo, etc.

'''blunting''' (blun′ting), ''n.''   [Verbal n. of ''blunt'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' The act of dulling.—'''2.''' Something that dulls or blunts. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Not impediments or ''bluntings'', but rather as whetstones, to set an edge on our desires.{{right|''Jer. Taylor'' (?), Artif. Handsomeness, p. 73.}}}}

'''bluntish''' (blun′tish), ''a.''   [< ''blunt'' + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.]   Somewhat blunt.

'''bluntishness''' (blun′tish-nes), ''n.''   [< ''bluntish'' + ''-ness''.]   A slight degree of bluntness.
{{smaller block|Tempered with an honest ''bluntishness''.{{right|''Wood'', Athenæ Oxon. (ed. 1815), II. 582.}}}}

'''bluntly''' (blunt′li), ''adv.'' '''1†.''' Stupidly.—'''2.''' Without sharpness or tenuity; obtusely: as, ''bluntly'' serrate.—'''3.''' In a blunt manner; abruptly; without delicacy, or the usual forms of civility; in an abrupt, offhand, or curt manner; without circumlocution: as, to tell a man something ''bluntly.''

<poem>Fathers are
Won by degrees, not ''bluntly'' as our masters
Or wronged friends are.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Dekker and Ford,'' Witch of Edmonton, i. 1.}}}}

'''bluntness''' (blunt′nes), ''n.''   [< ''blunt'' + ''-ness.'']   The state or quality of being blunt. {{smaller|(''a'') Want of sharpness; dullness; obtuseness. (''b'') Plainness, directness, or abruptness of address; want of ceremony in manners; rudeness of manner or address: as, “honest ''bluntness,''” ''Dryden;'' “''bluntness'' of speech,” ''Boyle.''}}

{{smaller block|To keep up Friendship, there must be little Addresses and Applications, whereas ''Bluntness'' spoils it quickly.
{{right|''Selden,'' Table-Talk, p. 23.}}}}

'''blunt-witted''' (blunt′wit″ed), ''a.''   [< ''blunt'' + ''wit'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>. Cf. ME. “blunt of wytte,” Prompt. Parv.]   Dull; stupid.

{{smaller block|''Blunt-witted'' lord, ignoble in demeanour!
{{right|''Shak.,'' 2 Hen. VI., iii. 2.}}}}

'''blur''' (blėr), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''blurred,'' ppr. ''blurring.''   [= Sc. ''blore;'' first in early mod. E. ''blurre;'' perhaps a deflected form of ''blear,'' early mod. E. ''blere'' (see ''blear''<sup>1</sup>), but it may be an independent formation. Cf. ''blot''<sup>1</sup>, ''blotch.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To ob'''2.''' To sully, stain, blemish: as, to ''blur'' one’s reputation.
{{smaller block|<poem>Never yet did base dishonour ''blur'' our name,
But with our sword we wip’d away the blot.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iv. 1.}}}}
'''3.''' To obscure without quite effacing; render indistinct; confuse and bedim, as the outlines of a figure.
{{smaller block|<poem>One low light betwixt them burn’d,
''Blurr’d'' by the creeping mist.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Guinevere.}}}}
'''4.''' To dim the perception or susceptibility of; make dull or insensible to impression: as, ''blurred'' eyesight; to ''blur'' the judgment.
{{smaller block|Her eyes are ''blurred'' with the lightning’s glare.
{{right|''N. Drake.''}}}}
{{smaller|'''To blur out''', to efface.}}
{{smaller block|We saw forked flashes once and again . . . lighting up the valleys for a moment, and leaving the darkness blacker . . . as the storm ''blurred out'' the landscape forty miles away.
{{right|''J. A. Symonds'', Italy and Greece, p. 228.}}}}
{{smaller|'''To blur over''', to obscure by a blur; put out of sight.}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To make blurs in writing.

'''blur''' (blėr), ''n.''   [< ''blur'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' A smudge or smear, such as that made by brushing writing or painting before it is dry; a blot which partially defaces or obscures.—'''2.''' Figuratively, a blot, stain, or injury affecting character, reputation, and the like.
{{smaller block|Her raillyng sette a greate ''blurre'' on myne honestie and good name.
{{right|''Udall'', tr. of Erasmus, Luke xviii.}}}}
{{smaller block|These ''blurs'' are too apparent in his Life.
{{right|''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., i.}}}}
'''3.''' A blurred condition; a dim, confused appearance; indistinctness. {{smaller block|The eye learns to discriminate colors, and shades of color, where at first there was only a vague ''blur'' of feeling.
{{right|''G. H. Lewes'', Probs. of Life and Mind, II. ii. § 10.}}}}

'''blurry''' (blėr′i), ''a.''   [< ''blur'', ''n.'', + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   Full of blurs; confused and indistinct.

'''blurt''' (blėrt), ''v.''   [= Sc. ''blirt'' (see ''blirt''); appar. imitative, with the initial sound as in ''blow''<sup>1</sup>, ''blast'', ''blash'', ''bluster'', etc., and the final sound as in ''spurt'', ''spirt'', ''squirt'', etc.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To utter suddenly or inadvertently; divulge unadvisedly: commonly with ''out''.
{{smaller block|Others . . . cannot hold, but ''blurt out'' those words which afterwards they are forced to eat.
{{right|''Hakewill.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And yet the truth may lose its grace,
If ''blurted'' to a person’s face.</poem>
{{right|''Lloyd'', The Nightingale.}}}}
{{smaller block|At last to ''blurt out'' the broad, staring question of, “Madam, will you marry me?”
{{right|''Goldsmith'', She Stoops to Conquer, ii.}}}}
'''2†.''' To treat contemptuously.
{{smaller block|<poem>And, I confess, I never was so ''blurted'',
Nor never so abus’d.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Wildgoose Chase, ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller|'''To blurt at†''', to speak contemptuously of; ridicule.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>None would look on her,
But cast their gazes on Marina’s face;
Whilst ours was ''blurted at.'' ''Shak.'', Pericles, iv. 4.</poem>}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To puff or emit the breath explosively as in sleep, or contemptuously as in saying “pooh”; puff in scorn or with a contemptuous expression of the lips.—'''2.''' To burst out weeping.
